document.title: CC CPSU Politburo Session March 17-18, 1979
document.publisher: National Security Archive (GWU), Afghanistan: Lessons from the Last War
document.note: Politburo session convened urgently after the Herat uprising, in which Soviet advisers were killed. Nearly all members opposed sending troops, though some argued the USSR could not lose Afghanistan. Brezhnev summed up that economic and military aid and advisers would be provided but no Soviet troops.

persons.role: General Secretary of the CPSU; presiding over Politburo session

under no circumstances may we lose Afghanistan

persons.name: Y. V. Andropov
persons.role: Chairman of the KGB; Politburo member

mentions.quote: Our operational data tells us that about three thousand insurgents are being directed into Afghanistan from Pakistan.

persons.name: A. N. Kosygin

mentions.quote: we must not delay the supply of armaments until April but must give them everything now
I think it is best for Comrade Kosygin to speak with Taraki.
I just spoke with Comrade Gorelov by telephone
We have prepared two options in respect to military action.

persons.role: CPSU Politburo attendee/Secretary for International Department

mentions.quote: We should send around 500 persons into Afghanistan in the capacity as advisors and specialists.

mentions.quote: we must finalize the political statement, bearing in mind that we will be labeled as an aggressor, but that under no circumstances can we lose Afghanistan.

we must decide who will invite Comrade Taraki.
I have signed documents authorizing the delivery of additional supplies of special materials, including military property and armaments
the time is not right for us to become entangled in that war

events.description: Politburo session on the deterioration of conditions in the DRA and possible aid.
Herat uprising: 17th Division collapses; artillery regiment and infantry regiment go over to insurgents; over a thousand reported killed.
Gromyko telephone conversation with Amin at 11:00, in which Amin downplayed the situation.
Taraki summoned Gorelov and Alekseev and requested military equipment, ammunition, rations, and possibly ground and air support.
Afghan operative groups to be deployed into Herat; Politburo to reconvene with Brezhnev and Kosygin to finalize aid decision.
Politburo session on Afghanistan; decisions on aid, a political document, warning to Pakistan, deployment of two divisions on border.
Kosygin phoned Taraki twice; Taraki asked for tanks and Tajik crews in Afghan uniforms.
Second session: troop deployment ruled out; decision to invite Taraki to Moscow.
Herat uprising; 17th division partly goes over to rebels.
Politburo session decides against sending troops, approves aid and warnings to Pakistan and Iran
Kosygin phone calls with Taraki, who requests troops for Herat
Herat uprising, with part of the government division joining insurgents
Decision to bring Taraki to Moscow for talks
Politburo session resolves measures on Afghanistan: Kosygin to call Taraki, draft political document, appeal to Pakistan, send specialists, deploy two divisions on border, publicity campaign.
Kirilenko contacts Chernenko during recess to relay Politburo proposals; session adjourned.
Kosygin telephones Taraki twice; Taraki asks for Soviet help including tanks and Tajik crews in Afghan uniforms for Herat; Kosygin refuses concealment.
Herat uprising: insurgent soldiers fraternizing with supporters; part of 17th Division (artillery, infantry regiment, antiaircraft battalion) defect to rebels.
Second day of Politburo session; Kosygin reports on his conversations with Taraki.
Kosygin's discussion with Hafizullah Amin; Amin denies threats to the regime.
Herat uprising: an artillery regiment fired on its own troops and part of a second regiment defected to insurgents; 17th Division largely ineffective.
Taraki summoned Gorelov and Alekseev and appealed for Soviet military equipment, ammunition, rations and possibly ground and air support.
Operative groups to be deployed into Herat.
Politburo agrees to give arms free of charge, drop the 25 percent assessment, raise gas price to 25 rubles, and increase bread supply from 75 to 100 thousand tons; ship all arms in March.
Kosygin proposes sending more military specialists, preparing a political decision, and not pressuring Afghan government to request Soviet troops.
Politburo session concludes: decide to keep aid but rule out troop deployment, invite Taraki, publish propaganda on Pakistan and China.
Herat uprising; part of Afghan division joins insurgents, over a thousand killed per Gromyko.
Amin urges Ustinov to deploy Soviet troops to Herat.
Taraki tells Kosygin that Herat will fall and requests troops; claims 4,000 Pakistani-sent men in Afghan uniforms.
Mass demonstration in Kabul in support of the government.
Afghan government publishes a proclamation against Pakistan, judged not strident enough.
Brezhnev signs documents authorizing additional military supplies and political measures; judges troop deployment inadvisable.
Massive pro-government demonstration in Kabul.
Kosygin spoke twice with Taraki; Taraki asked for troops, said Herat would fall.
Ustinov spoke with Amin, who asked for tanks and complained of Pakistani/Iranian saboteurs.
Politburo approves measures on Afghanistan, rejects troop deployment, and orders warning letters to Pakistan and Iran.
Brezhnev ordered letters to Pakistan and Iran sent the same day.
Decision to bring Taraki to Moscow March 20 for talks with Kosygin, Gromyko, Ustinov, then Brezhnev.
Politburo session on deteriorating situation in Afghanistan, chaired by Brezhnev; proposals prepared by Gromyko, Andropov and Ustinov.
Herat uprising: the Afghan 17th Division collapsed, with an artillery regiment and an infantry regiment going over to insurgents.
Gromyko's 11:00 call with Amin; Amin said the situation was under control.
Soviet appropriation of an additional 10 million rubles in hard currency for Afghan border protection.
Taraki summoned Gorelov and Alekseev and requested Soviet equipment and possibly ground and air support.
Operative groups were to be deployed into Herat.
Politburo reverses its stance and rules out deploying Soviet troops to Afghanistan, agreeing to continue other aid.
Reports that a division/regiments of the 17th Division in Herat went over to the rebels.
Taraki tells Kosygin by phone that the army is too small and requests Soviet assistance.
Amin tells Ustinov the revolution's survival depends on the Soviet Union and requests forces for Herat.
Decision to invite Taraki to Moscow and send a plane to Kabul.
Politburo discusses two military options for Afghanistan, political decision, and talks with Taraki.
Proposal to send around 500 advisors/specialists to Afghanistan; about 550 already there.
Kosygin to consult Brezhnev next day, then speak with Taraki.

relationships.detail: Kirilenko opened the session on Brezhnev's behalf as a Politburo member.
relationships.quote: Leonid Ilych [Brezhnev] has asked us to commence our Politburo session today at this unseasonable hour

relationships.detail: Gromyko attended the Politburo session.
relationships.quote: In attendance: Y. V. ANDROPOV, A. A. GROMYKO, A. N. KOSYGIN

relationships.detail: Andropov attended the Politburo session.
relationships.quote: In attendance: Y. V. ANDROPOV, A. A. GROMYKO

relationships.detail: Ustinov attended the Politburo session.
relationships.quote: CHERNENKO, D. F. USTINOV, P. N. DEMICHEV

relationships.detail: Gromyko, Andropov and Ustinov jointly prepared proposals on Afghanistan.
relationships.quote: Comrades Gromyko, Andropov and Ustinov today have put together some proposals

relationships.detail: Joint drafting of proposals on Afghanistan.
relationships.quote: Comrades Gromyko, Andropov and Ustinov today have put together some proposals

relationships.detail: Joint drafting of proposals on Afghanistan.
relationships.quote: Comrades Gromyko, Andropov and Ustinov today have put together some proposals

relationships.detail: Gorelov is the chief Soviet military advisor in Afghanistan.
relationships.quote: our chief military advisor Comrade Gorelov

relationships.detail: Alekseev is temporary chargé d'affaires in Afghanistan.
relationships.quote: temporary chargé d'affaires Comrade Alekseev

relationships.detail: Gorelov was in Afghanistan, meeting Taraki.
relationships.quote: Comrade Gorelov, our chief military advisor, was with Taraki along with Comrade Alekseev

relationships.detail: An artillery and an infantry regiment of the 17th Division went over to the insurgents.
relationships.quote: An artillery regiment and one infantry regiment comprising that division have gone over to the side of the insurgents.

relationships.detail: Insurgents infiltrated Herat Province from Pakistan and Iran.
relationships.quote: The insurgents infiltrating into the territory of Herat Province from Pakistan and Iran have joined forces with a domestic counter-revolution.

relationships.detail: Amin is Taraki's deputy and foreign minister.
relationships.quote: Amin -- Taraki's deputy who is the minister of foreign affairs

relationships.detail: Gromyko spoke with Amin by telephone at 11:00 on March 17.
relationships.quote: I had a conversation this morning at 11:00 with Amin

relationships.detail: Ustinov spoke with Gorelov by telephone.
relationships.quote: I just spoke with Comrade Gorelov by telephone

relationships.detail: Taraki told Kosygin that if Herat falls the revolution is doomed, and if it holds survival is assured.
relationships.quote: if Herat falls, then the revolution is doomed. And on the contrary, if it holds out, then survival of the revolution is assured.

relationships.detail: Amin appealed to Ustinov for assistance, saying survival depends on the Soviet Union.
relationships.quote: its survival now depends totally on the Soviet Union.

relationships.detail: Kosygin conversed with Taraki, who asked for Soviet assistance.
relationships.quote: Your assistance is required, Comrade Taraki again declared.

relationships.detail: Kosygin proposed instructing ambassador Vinogradov to warn Bazargan.
relationships.quote: we ought to instruct our ambassador, Comrade Vinogradov, to go to Prime Minister of Iran Bazargan

relationships.detail: Proposed meeting to warn that interference in Afghanistan is intolerable.
relationships.quote: inform him that interference in the internal affairs of Afghanistan cannot be tolerated.

relationships.detail: Gromyko fully supported Andropov's proposal to rule out deploying troops.
relationships.quote: I completely support Comrade Andropov's proposal to rule out such a measure as the deployment of our troops into Afghanistan

relationships.detail: Politburo proposed inviting Taraki to Moscow.
relationships.quote: invite Comrade Taraki to Moscow and tell him about everything that we have agreed on.

relationships.detail: Andropov proposed telling Taraki that USSR supports all measures except troop deployment.
relationships.quote: We should state directly to Comrade Taraki that we will support you with all measures and means except for the deployment of troops.

relationships.detail: Kosygin says Amin and Taraki conceal the true state of affairs in Afghanistan from Moscow.
relationships.quote: Amin and Taraki alike are concealing from us the true state of affairs.

relationships.detail: Kosygin says Taraki conceals the true state of affairs; Kosygin is to speak with him.
relationships.quote: Amin and Taraki alike are concealing from us the true state of affairs.

relationships.detail: Kosygin predicts Iran, China and Pakistan will oppose the Afghan government.
relationships.quote: Iran, China and Pakistan will come out against Afghanistan

relationships.detail: Predicted opposition to Afghan government.
relationships.quote: Iran, China and Pakistan will come out against Afghanistan

relationships.detail: Predicted opposition to Afghan government.
relationships.quote: Iran, China and Pakistan will come out against Afghanistan

relationships.detail: Carter is expected to oppose the Afghan leadership.
relationships.quote: Carter will also come out against the leadership of Afghanistan.

relationships.detail: Option one: deploy 105th airborne division into Afghanistan in a single day.
relationships.quote: deploy into Afghanistan the 105th airborne division

relationships.detail: Planned to be placed toward the border.
relationships.quote: toward the border we would place the 68th motorized division

relationships.detail: Would be located at the border.
relationships.quote: the 5th motor artillery division would be located at the border.

relationships.detail: Ustinov presents Defense plans for military options.
relationships.quote: We have prepared two options in respect to military action.

relationships.detail: Kirilenko says Taraki must be instructed to change tactics and request troops.
relationships.quote: we must bear upon Taraki

relationships.detail: Agreed that Kosygin should speak with Taraki.
relationships.quote: It is better for Comrade Kosygin to speak with him.

relationships.detail: Andropov says bands are streaming in from Pakistan.
relationships.quote: bands are streaming in from Pakistan.

relationships.detail: Advisors assist the Afghan army.
relationships.quote: with the assistance of our advisors, there is much that the army can do.

relationships.detail: Ponomarev says the army achieved the coup and could defend the country.
relationships.quote: The Afghan army achieved a revolutionary coup d'état

key_claims: Soviet leaders believed insurgents in Herat were trained and armed in Pakistan and Iran, with Chinese and US involvement.
Gromyko declared that under no circumstances could the USSR lose Afghanistan.
Taraki hinted that Soviet ground and air forces might be required.
Kosygin criticized Taraki and Amin for concealing the true situation and for executing Parcham leaders.
Ustinov outlined options to deploy the 105th Airborne Division or two divisions, contingent on a political decision.
Kirilenko insisted that Soviet troops cannot be deployed without an Afghan government request and that Taraki must curb mass repression of religious communities.
The Politburo ruled out deploying Soviet troops to Afghanistan on 18 March 1979 while continuing arms and advisor support.
Soviet leaders blamed Pakistan, Iran, China and the US for supporting the Afghan insurgents and planned a press campaign.
Taraki said the Herat uprising threatened the regime and requested tanks and Tajik crews in Afghan uniforms.
Ustinov reported that Afghan leaders underestimated Islamic fundamentalism, with soldiers mutinying under Islamic banners.
Andropov and Gromyko argued that intervention would fight the Afghan people, harming détente and relations with China and non-aligned states.
The Politburo authorized deploying two divisions on the Soviet-Afghan border.
The Politburo rejected direct troop deployment in March 1979, fearing damage to détente, SALT-II and Western relations.
Soviet leaders attributed the Herat uprising to insurgents sent from Pakistan and Iran, directed by the USA with Chinese involvement.
Taraki and Amin repeatedly requested Soviet troops and tanks for Herat.
Soviets planned increased arms, advisors, interpreters and officer training, plus warnings to Pakistan and Iran.
Andropov criticized the Afghan leadership for executing opponents and failing to broaden its base.
Soviet military readiness measures included forming divisions in Turkestan and Central Asian districts.
